ground_truth.summary: Motion means an object changes its position over time. We describe motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors, which means they carry direction. Motion can be uniform or accelerated, and graphs of distance against time make these quantities easy to read. This page builds each idea slowly with small examples.

claims.statement: Motion is the change in position of an object with time.
Distance is the total path length and is a scalar; displacement is the shortest straight-line change from start to end and is a vector.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and its SI unit is m/s2.
If a body starts from rest and gains a speed of 10 m/s in 5 s, its acceleration is 2 m/s2.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time; for example 100 m covered in 20 s gives an average speed of 5 m/s.
The slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed of the object.
Displacement and velocity are vector quantities because they carry direction.

key_terms.definition: the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the final point, together with its direction
speed in a particular direction; the rate of change of displacement
the rate of change of velocity with time
motion in which the object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time

equations.description: final velocity from initial velocity u, acceleration a and time t

misconceptions.wrong_belief: distance and displacement are always equal
misconceptions.correction: they are equal only when the path is a straight line with no turning back

lesson.title: Motion: describing how things move
objectives: After this lesson you can explain what motion, distance and displacement mean.
After this lesson you can calculate speed, velocity and acceleration using simple formulas.
After this lesson you can read a distance-time graph and say how fast something moves.

sections.title: What motion means
paragraphs: You are in motion when your position changes with time. A bus moving down a road is in motion, and so is a fan blade going around. To say that something moved, we compare its position now with its position a moment ago.
To describe motion clearly we use a few measured quantities. Each one answers a different question: how far, how fast, and speeding up or slowing down. You will meet them one at a time.

sections.title: Distance and displacement
paragraphs: Distance is the total length of the path you travelled. Walk 3 metres forward and then 4 metres back, and your distance is 7 metres. Distance only has a size, so it is called a scalar.

Displacement is the shortest straight line from your starting point to your ending point, with its direction. In the same walk you end up 1 metre behind where you began, so your displacement is 1 metre backwards. Because it carries a direction, displacement is a vector.
Distance and displacement are equal only when the whole path is one straight line with no turning back. The moment you turn, they separate.

sections.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
paragraphs: Speed tells you how much distance is covered in each second. It is distance divided by time. Cover 100 metres in 20 seconds and your average speed is 5 m/s.
Velocity is speed with a direction attached. A car moving north at 20 m/s and a car moving south at 20 m/s have the same speed but different velocities.

Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. If a body at rest reaches a speed of 10 m/s in 5 seconds, its velocity changed by 10 m/s in 5 s, so its acceleration is 2 m/s2. A common formula is v = u + a*t, where u is the starting velocity.

sections.title: Reading motion from graphs
paragraphs: A distance-time graph plots distance on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. The slope of the line tells you the speed: a steep slope means fast motion and a flat line means the object is at rest.
For steady motion the graph is a straight line. When the line curves, the speed is changing, which means the motion is accelerated.

glossary.definition: the shortest straight-line distance from start to end, with its direction

a quantity that has only a size, such as distance or speed
a quantity that has both size and direction, such as displacement or velocity

spec.problem: A body starts from rest and accelerates steadily. It gains a speed of 10 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?

steps.title: Write what you know
steps.detail: Starting velocity u = 0 because the body starts from rest, final velocity v = 10 m/s, time t = 5 s.

steps.title: Choose the relation
steps.detail: Use v = u + a*t, which connects velocity change to acceleration and time.

spec.question: Which quantity is defined as the rate of change of velocity?
spec.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time; its SI unit is m/s2.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can name acceleration as the quantity that measures changing velocity.

spec.title: Motion with steady acceleration
spec.description: A dot starts at rest and speeds up. Increase or decrease the acceleration and watch how the dot covers distance.
spec.learning_goal: Connect the size of acceleration to how quickly the dot crosses the canvas.
spec.default_behaviour: The dot starts from rest and drifts faster to the right while the acceleration is positive.

spec.question: A cycle covers 100 m in 20 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
spec.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time: 100 / 20.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can compute average speed from distance and time.

spec.question: Which of these is a vector quantity?
spec.explanation: Displacement carries a direction from start to end, so it is a vector; distance, mass and time have only size.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can tell scalars and vectors apart for the quantities on this page.
